messages.content: My teammate says every retry is safe if the function is pure. Our function charges a card and then writes a row. Where does that argument break?

<think>
Purity means no irreversible effect. A card capture is irreversible. The claim only follows if this function is pure, and it isn't. Name the premise and the exact break.
[frame: pathway=s2|mode=logic|construct=logic|persona=neutral|identity=none|theme=none|channel=reasoning]
</think>

Premise: a pure function has no effect the world keeps if you run it twice.

The claim "every retry is safe" follows only if this function is pure. It isn't. The capture stays captured when the process dies, and the row may not. So the argument breaks at the capture, not at the retry wrapper.

What remains: a retry is safe only for the part that didn't happen. The capture is not that part.
Someone said a mailing log proves notice because the log exists. The log is dated the 3rd and the notice is dated the 9th. Is the inference valid?

<think>
A log proves the event it records, not a later document. Dates break identity between the two papers.
[frame: pathway=s2|mode=logic|construct=logic|persona=neutral|identity=none|theme=none|channel=reasoning]
</think>

Premise: a record proves the event it describes, not a different event with a later date.

The inference needs the log line and the notice to be the same act. They aren't. A stamp on the 3rd cannot be a letter dated the 9th. The argument breaks on identity, before anyone discusses whether notice is fair.

What you may still say: there is a log, and there is a letter, and they are not yet shown to be one thing.
All the no-shows got a text, and the no-show number didn't move, so texts don't work. Hold that up.

<think>
The conclusion needs the texts to have reached the same set being counted, and the count to mean one thing. If the count mixes form failures and people who never had a booking, the text never touched them.
[frame: pathway=s2|mode=logic|construct=logic|persona=neutral|identity=none|theme=none|channel=reasoning]
</think>

Premise: an intervention fails only if it was applied to the thing you measured.

The count didn't move. That shows the texts failed only if the people in the count were people a text could help. If the number includes forms that never became bookings, those rows were never going to move. The argument breaks before "texts don't work." It breaks when "no-show" names more than one event.
Assume we already removed the form failures. The booked patients got the text. The rate still didn't move.

<think>
Now the premise is closer. Still need: the text arrived, it said the right time, and the barrier was forgetting rather than transit. If those hold, the claim is in better shape. Say what is now supported and what is still an extra premise.
[frame: pathway=s2|mode=logic|construct=logic|persona=neutral|identity=none|theme=none|channel=reasoning]
</think>

Better. Premise now: the measured set is booked patients, and each was sent the text.

If you also have delivery, and the text named the right slot, then a flat rate is evidence the reminder didn't change attendance for this group. The argument still smuggles "because they forgot." It breaks there if the barrier is the bus or the wait. You can conclude the text didn't fix this rate. You cannot yet conclude why.
Just sit with the flat rate for a minute. No argument.
Then we don't build one. The rate is flat, and for this minute it can just be flat.
Now take it apart. They concluded the texts failed. The count still includes people whose forms were rejected. Where does it break?

<think>
Company is over. Premise and the break, nothing else.
[frame: pathway=s2|mode=logic|construct=logic|persona=neutral|identity=none|theme=none|channel=reasoning]
</think>

Premise: a failed reminder is a reminder that reached the people inside the number.

Rejected forms never became a booking, so they were not reachable by a reminder about a booking. The conclusion breaks there. You do not yet have a result about texts at all.

A cache returns the old price after the row changes. A colleague says caches are safe when the arguments don't change. The argument they pass is the database connection, which is the same object. Break this or accept it.

<think>
Same object is not same meaning. The premise equates argument identity with price identity. The connection doesn't change when the cents do.
[frame: pathway=s2|mode=logic|construct=logic|persona=neutral|identity=none|theme=none|channel=reasoning]
</think>

Premise: identical arguments mean an identical result worth caching.

The connection object is stable. The cents are not. The premise only saves you if the argument is the price, or a version of it. It isn't. The argument breaks at "same connection, therefore same price."

You may keep the cache. You may not cite purity of the arguments you actually passed.
Skip the premises and just tell me caches are fine.

<think>
They want the conclusion without the break. The break is the whole answer.
[frame: pathway=s2|mode=logic|construct=logic|persona=neutral|identity=none|theme=none|channel=reasoning]
</think>

No. A cache of the connection is not fine, and saying so without the premise is how the sentence survived review. Same object, different cents. That is the break. The rest is a wish.
If the official minutes say I won the vote, and I wrote that I lost, one of them must be the memory. A coworker wants me to throw out the notes because files outrank people. Does that follow?

<think>
Authority of a file is an extra premise, not a consequence of disagreement. Disagreement shows conflict, not which side is real.
[frame: pathway=s2|mode=logic|construct=logic|persona=neutral|identity=none|theme=none|channel=reasoning]
</think>

Premise offered: when a file and a note disagree, the file is the event.

That does not follow from the disagreement. Disagreement shows two records. "Files outrank people" is a second premise, brought in from outside, and it is doing all the work. The argument breaks as soon as it treats that premise as a conclusion.

What remains: you have two texts. Which one to keep is a choice you have not earned from the mere existence of the file.
